claim: DUX4 is a transcription factor whose misexpression in skeletal muscle causes facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy (FSHD).
source: DUX4 is a transcription factor whose misexpression in skeletal muscle causes facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy (FSHD).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature (Tawil et al., 2014; Lemmers et al., 2010) in the Introduction section.

claim: DUX4 transcriptional targets were robustly translated in DUX4-expressing cells.
source: DUX4 transcriptional targets were robustly translated, confirming the likely clinical relevance of proposed FSHD biomarkers.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative mass spectrometry data showing protein expression of DUX4 targets, as shown in Figure 1D,E.

claim: A multitude of mRNAs and proteins exhibited discordant expression changes upon DUX4 expression.
source: However, a multitude of mRNAs and proteins exhibited discordant expression changes upon DUX4 expression.
evidence: This claim is supported by the comparison of RNA-seq and proteomics data showing different fold changes at RNA vs protein levels, as illustrated in Figure 2B.

claim: DUX4 expression causes Golgi apparatus fragmentation.
source: We found that DUX4-expressing cells showed severe fragmentation of their Golgi apparatus, which could be an indicator of a perturbation in the cellular secretory pathways (Bexiga and Simpson, 2013) (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 2D and quantification in Figure 2E.

claim: Key components of RNA degradation machineries, including UPF1, UPF3B, and XRN1, exhibited suppressed protein, but not mRNA, levels in DUX4-expressing cells.
source: Key components of RNA degradation machineries, including UPF1, UPF3B, and XRN1, exhibited suppressed protein, but not mRNA, levels, explaining the build-up of aberrant RNAs that characterizes DUX4-expressing cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by proteomics and RNA-seq data showing discordant changes, as illustrated in Figure 4B.

claim: Transient and pulsatile expression of DUX4 is sufficient to induce pathology and cell death.
source: As transient and pulsatile expression of DUX4 is sufficient to induce pathology and cell death (Rickard et al., 2015), it is critical that we understand the cellular events and pathways set in motion by DUX4 that lead to eventual cell death, in order to develop effective therapeutics for FSHD.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Rickard et al., 2015.

claim: DUX4 induces changes in the expression of hundreds of genes that impact dozens of highly interconnected pathways.
source: DUX4 induces changes in the expression of hundreds of genes that impact dozens of highly interconnected pathways (Geng et al., 2012; Block et al., 2013; Young et al., 2013; Banerji et al., 2015; Feng et al., 2015; Homma et al., 2015; Dmitriev et al., 2016; Shadle et al., 2017), making a cause-and-effect relationship between dysregulated gene expression and FSHD pathology difficult to discern.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: RNA and protein levels are not always concordant and post-transcriptional regulation can result in divergent RNA and protein levels.
source: Although this is a reasonable assumption, it is well known that RNA and protein levels are not always concordant and that post-transcriptional regulation can result in divergent RNA and protein levels (Schwanhäusser et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Schwanhäusser et al., 2011 and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: DUX4 induces the proteolysis of UPF1.
source: Furthermore, given our recent discovery that DUX4 induces the proteolysis of a key RNA-binding protein, UPF1 (7), we hypothesized that paired measurements of RNA and protein levels might be particularly important in identifying altered post-transcriptional gene regulation in DUX4-expressing cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work (reference 7, which is Feng et al., 2015).

claim: SILAC labeling efficiency was greater than 95% in MB135 myoblasts after one week of labeling.
source: First, we quantified the relative abundance of heavy and light spectra for several individual peptides and found that it showed a > 95% labeling efficiency (a representative example is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: 65 genes were identified as potential FSHD biomarkers by Yao et al. (2014) based on transcriptome analysis of FSHD patient samples.
source: Moreover, of the 65 genes identified by Yao et al. (2014) as potential FSHD biomarkers on the basis of transcriptome analysis of FSHD patient samples, 8 were quantified in the vDUX4 proteomics study and 25 were quantified in the iDUX4 proteomics study and all of these genes show high induction at the protein level (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Yao et al. (2014) and proteomics data shown in Figure 1D,E.

claim: All FSHD biomarker genes quantified in the proteomics studies showed high induction at the protein level.
source: Moreover, of the 65 genes identified by Yao et al. (2014) as potential FSHD biomarkers on the basis of transcriptome analysis of FSHD patient samples, 8 were quantified in the vDUX4 proteomics study and 25 were quantified in the iDUX4 proteomics study and all of these genes show high induction at the protein level (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by proteomics data shown in Figure 1D,E.

claim: Quantitative proteomics information was obtained for 4005 genes in the iDUX4 dataset.
source: After filtering out genes that were only observed in one of the two label-swap replicates, we obtained quantitative proteomics information for 4005 genes, 3961 of which also had a corresponding RNA-seq measurement (Figure 2A; RNA-seq data previously reported by Jagannathan et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data analysis described in the methods and results.

claim: 3961 genes had both proteomics and RNA-seq measurements in the iDUX4 dataset.
source: After filtering out genes that were only observed in one of the two label-swap replicates, we obtained quantitative proteomics information for 4005 genes, 3961 of which also had a corresponding RNA-seq measurement (Figure 2A; RNA-seq data previously reported by Jagannathan et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data analysis described in the methods and results.

claim: Among genes upregulated more than 4-fold, the concordance between RNA and protein was roughly 40-50%.
source: Among genes that are upregulated (>2 log2 fold change), the concordance between RNA and protein was roughly 40–50%, whereas similarly downregulated genes show very little concordance (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the overlap analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The Pearson's correlation coefficient between RNA and protein fold changes was 0.51 (p-value<2.2e-16).
source: We found a reasonable level of correlation between these values with a Pearson's correlation coefficient, r, of 0.51 (p-value<2.2e-16).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the RNA-seq and proteomics data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Transcript level changes occur in genes involved in transcription and mRNA processing.
source: Transcript level changes occur in genes that are involved in transcription and mRNA processing, whereas protein-level changes impact pathways including the humoral immune response, proteolysis and exocytosis.
evidence: This claim is supported by Gene Ontology analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Protein-level changes impact pathways including the humoral immune response, proteolysis and exocytosis.
source: Transcript level changes occur in genes that are involved in transcription and mRNA processing, whereas protein-level changes impact pathways including the humoral immune response, proteolysis and exocytosis.
evidence: This claim is supported by Gene Ontology analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The exocytosis pathway was not implicated in previous studies of DUX4 gene expression.
source: The exocytosis pathway was not implicated in any of the previous studies of DUX4 gene expression, so we sought to examine this phenomenon further by imaging the Golgi apparatus, which is the source of exocytotic vesicles in the cell (Rodriguez-Boulan and Müsch, 2005).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the literature and citation to Rodriguez-Boulan and Müsch, 2005.

claim: The Golgi apparatus is the source of exocytotic vesicles in the cell.
source: The exocytosis pathway was not implicated in any of the previous studies of DUX4 gene expression, so we sought to examine this phenomenon further by imaging the Golgi apparatus, which is the source of exocytotic vesicles in the cell (Rodriguez-Boulan and Müsch, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Rodriguez-Boulan and Müsch, 2005 and represents established knowledge.

claim: Golgi apparatus fragmentation could be an indicator of perturbation in cellular secretory pathways.
source: We found that DUX4-expressing cells showed severe fragmentation of their Golgi apparatus, which could be an indicator of a perturbation in the cellular secretory pathways (Bexiga and Simpson, 2013) (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Bexiga and Simpson, 2013.

claim: The percentage of cells with DUX4 expression was comparable to the percentage of cells with fragmented Golgi.
source: We found the percentages of cells with DUX4 expression to be comparable to the percentage of cells with fragmented Golgi (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: 678 genes showed post-transcriptional buffering with significant changes at the transcript level but no change in protein level.
source: Although many of the genes that are induced at the transcript level are largely also induced at the protein-level, a subset of genes showed no change in their protein level while their transcripts were up- or downregulated to a significant degree (678 genes, shaded blue in Figure 3A), indicating post-transcriptional buffering of the protein levels.
evidence: This claim is supported by the scatter plot analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Several housekeeping genes that respond to protein folding stress or dsRNA-induced stress showed transcriptional upregulation with minimal protein-level upregulation.
source: Most notably, several housekeeping genes that respond to protein folding stress or dsRNA-induced stress showed transcriptional upregulation with minimal protein-level upregulation (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Both unfolded protein and dsRNA-induced stresses converge in the phosphorylation of eIF2α and lead to translation inhibition.
source: Given that both unfolded protein and dsRNA-induced stresses converge in the phosphorylation of eIF2a and lead to translation inhibition (Cláudio et al., 2013), we asked whether the timing of the transcription of various stress-response genes coincideswith their translational downregulation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Cláudio et al., 2013 and represents established knowledge.

claim: HSPA5 is a prominent marker of the unfolded protein response pathway.
source: We found that HSPA5, a prominent marker of the unfolded protein response pathway (Oslowski and Urano, 2011), shows transcriptional upregulation during a time period that temporally coincides with eIF2a phosphorylation and the reduced incorporation of [35 S]-labeled methionine, a proxy for bulk translation efficiency (Figure 3C–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Oslowski and Urano, 2011.

claim: HSPA5 shows transcriptional upregulation during a time period that temporally coincides with eIF2α phosphorylation and reduced incorporation of [35S]-labeled methionine.
source: We found that HSPA5, a prominent marker of the unfolded protein response pathway (Oslowski and Urano, 2011), shows transcriptional upregulation during a time period that temporally coincides with eIF2a phosphorylation and the reduced incorporation of [35 S]-labeled methionine, a proxy for bulk translation efficiency (Figure 3C–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR, immunoblot, and methionine incorporation data shown in Figure 3C-E.

claim: Translation inhibition caused by cellular stresses and post-transcriptional buffering prevents DUX4-expressing cells from mounting a robust stress response.
source: These data demonstrate that translation inhibition caused by various cellular stresses and the resulting post-transcriptional buffering prevents DUX4-expressing cells from mounting a robust stress response.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the data showing transcriptional upregulation but translational buffering of stress response genes.

claim: 198 genes showed significant changes at the protein level with either no change or a change in the opposite direction in their transcript abundance.
source: Next, we focused our analysis on the subset of genes that showed significant changes at the protein level with either no change or a change in the opposite direction in their transcript abundance (198 genes shown as 'gold' circles in Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the scatter plot analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Many components of the nonsense-mediated RNA decay pathway, including UPF1, UPF2, UPF3B and XRN1, showed downregulation at the protein level.
source: Many of these genes, including UPF1, UPF2, UPF3B and XRN1, showed downregulation at the protein level.
evidence: This claim is supported by proteomics data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: XRN1 is the 5'-3' exonuclease that degrades NMD targets upon cleavage by the endonuclease SMG6.
source: The downregulation of XRN1 is of particular interest as it is the 5'−3' exonuclease that degrades NMD targets upon cleavage by the endonuclease, SMG6 (Palacios, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Palacios, 2013 and represents established knowledge.

claim: SMG6 is downregulated to a log2 fold change of -4.7 in DUX4-expressing cells.
source: Moreover, SMG6 too is downregulated to a log2 fold change of −4.7, although it is only detected as a single peptide and hence was filtered out of our analysis.
evidence: This claim is supported by proteomics data, though the protein was filtered out due to low peptide count.

claim: DUX4-induced NMD inhibition appears to be a result of the post-transcriptional downregulation of multiple key players of the NMD pathway.
source: Thus, DUX4-induced NMD inhibition appears to be a result of the post-transcriptional downregulation of multiple key players of the NMD pathway, which explains the severity of NMD inhibition in DUX4-expressing cells.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the proteomics data showing downregulation of multiple NMD pathway components.

claim: DUX4 induces proteasome-mediated degradation of UPF1.
source: We have previously shown that DUX4 induces proteasome-mediated degradation of UPF1 (Feng et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Feng et al., 2015).

claim: DUX4 affects the expression of several genes in the ubiquitin proteasome pathway.
source: A scatterplot of all ubiquitin proteasome regulators shows a change in the expression of several such genes, one or more of which may underlie the rapid degradation of UPF1 (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the scatter plot analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Post-transcriptional gene regulation plays a critical role in inhibiting NMD in DUX4-expressing cells.
source: In summary, we propose that post-transcriptional gene regulation plays a critical role in inhibiting NMD and in perturbing the proteostasis in DUX4-expressing cells, and thus may underlie key aspects of FSHD pathology (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the combined RNA-seq and proteomics data.

claim: Post-transcriptional gene regulation plays a critical role in perturbing proteostasis in DUX4-expressing cells.
source: In summary, we propose that post-transcriptional gene regulation plays a critical role in inhibiting NMD and in perturbing the proteostasis in DUX4-expressing cells, and thus may underlie key aspects of FSHD pathology (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the combined RNA-seq and proteomics data.

claim: Post-transcriptional gene regulation may underlie key aspects of FSHD pathology.
source: In summary, we propose that post-transcriptional gene regulation plays a critical role in inhibiting NMD and in perturbing the proteostasis in DUX4-expressing cells, and thus may underlie key aspects of FSHD pathology (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference from the data.

claim: Most highly induced DUX4 transcriptional targets are germline and early embryonic genes that are normally never expressed in adult muscle.
source: Most of the highly induced DUX4 transcriptional targets are germline and early embryonic genes that are normally never expressed in adult muscle (Geng et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Geng et al., 2012.

claim: DUX4-induced transcripts are efficiently translated into stable proteins in muscle cells.
source: Here, we used quantitative mass spectrometry in two different cell culture models of FSHD to demonstrate that DUX4-induced transcripts are efficiently translated into stable proteins in muscle cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by the proteomics data showing protein expression of DUX4 targets.

claim: The vDUX4 and iDUX4 systems accurately capture the transcriptional program of FSHD cells.
source: We demonstrated previously that our vDUX4 and iDUX4 systems accurately capture the transcriptional program of FSHD cells (Jagannathan et al., 2016), so it is reasonable to assume that DUX4-induced transcripts are similarly translated into stable proteins in FSHD muscle.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Jagannathan et al., 2016).

claim: DUX4-induced transcripts are likely translated into stable proteins in FSHD muscle.
source: We demonstrated previously that our vDUX4 and iDUX4 systems accurately capture the transcriptional program of FSHD cells (Jagannathan et al., 2016), so it is reasonable to assume that DUX4-induced transcripts are similarly translated into stable proteins in FSHD muscle.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the cell culture data and previous validation of the model systems.

claim: Further work is required to confirm definitively that DUX4-induced transcripts are translated into stable proteins in FSHD muscle.
source: However, further work is required to confirm this definitively.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of the limitations of the current study.

claim: The changes in the DUX4 proteome are not largely reflective of the changes to the transcriptome.
source: Next, we asked whether the changes in the DUX4 proteome are largely reflective of the changes to the transcriptome. We found that this is not the case.
evidence: This claim is supported by the correlation analysis showing r=0.51 between RNA and protein fold changes.

claim: Transcriptome-level analysis paints an incomplete picture of DUX4 biology.
source: We take these results as an indication that the transcriptome-level analysis paints an incomplete picture of DUX4 biology, which should be complemented with proteome-level analysis to provide a thorough understanding of how DUX4 misexpression causes FSHD.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the discordance between RNA and protein measurements.

claim: Genes induced by double-stranded RNA and unfolded protein stress are transcriptionally induced but translationally buffered in DUX4-expressing cells.
source: We found that genes that are induced by double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) and unfolded protein stress are transcriptionally induced, but translationally buffered as a result of the translational repression that accompanies activation of these stress-response pathways.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data showing transcriptional upregulation but minimal protein upregulation of stress response genes.

claim: DUX4-expressing cells are unable to mount a robust stress response despite inducing the transcripts necessary to alleviate stress.
source: Motivated by this result, we hypothesize that DUX4-expressing cells are unable to mount a robust stress response, despite inducing the transcripts necessary to alleviate stress.
evidence: This claim is a hypothesis based on the observation of post-transcriptional buffering of stress response genes.

claim: Multiple proteins in RNA surveillance pathways are downregulated at the protein level, which may explain the drastic reduction in RNA quality control capacity in DUX4-expressing cells.
source: We also show that multiple proteins in RNA surveillance pathways, including UPF1 and XRN1, are downregulated at the protein level, which may explain the drastic reduction in RNA quality control capacity that we observed in DUX4-expressing cells.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the proteomics data showing downregulation of RNA surveillance proteins.

claim: Proteomics has lower sensitivity than RNA-seq.
source: The lower number of genes quantified by proteomics compared to RNA-seq is expected as proteomics is known to have lower sensitivity than RNA-seq.
evidence: This represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: The two viral replicates showed strong correlation with a Pearson's r of 0.81.
source: Upon comparing the gene-level fold changes obtained from four different samples, we noticed a strong correlation between the two viral replicates (Pearson's r = 0.81), as well as the data from iDUX4 replicate 1 and both vDUX4 datasets (Pearson's r = 0.79 and 0.77).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the proteomics data.

claim: The iDUX4 replicate 1 showed strong correlation with both vDUX4 datasets (Pearson's r = 0.79 and 0.77).
source: Upon comparing the gene-level fold changes obtained from four different samples, we noticed a strong correlation between the two viral replicates (Pearson's r = 0.81), as well as the data from iDUX4 replicate 1 and both vDUX4 datasets (Pearson's r = 0.79 and 0.77).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the proteomics data.

claim: The iDUX4 replicate 2 showed poor correlation with the three other samples because of a small set of proteins (103 proteins; 2.6% of total) that did not label efficiently.
source: The iDUX4 replicate 2, in which we swapped the isotopic labels used for the control and DUX4 samples, however, showed poor correlation with the three other samples because of a small set of proteins (103 proteins; 2.6% of total) that did not label efficiently.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of the SILAC labeling efficiency in the proteomics data.

claim: Proteins that do not label efficiently result in apparent anticorrelation between label-swap samples.
source: Proteins that do not label efficiently result in apparent anticorrelation between label-swap samples. This issue, wherein a small subset of proteins does not label efficiently, is a well-known problem in SILAC experiments (Park et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Park et al., 2012 and represents established knowledge.

claim: A small subset of proteins not labeling efficiently is a well-known problem in SILAC experiments.
source: This issue, wherein a small subset of proteins does not label efficiently, is a well-known problem in SILAC experiments (Park et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Park et al., 2012.

claim: The median value of H/L ratio across the two iDUX4 replicates was taken as the final iDUX4 H/L ratio.
source: Rather than ignoring this subset of proteins, which would require the imposition of potentially arbitrary thresholds, we instead followed the standard SILAC analysis procedure of taking the median value of H/L ratio across the two iDUX4 replicates as the final iDUX4 H/L ratio (Park et al., 2012; Ong and Mann, 2006).
evidence: This claim describes the data analysis method used, supported by citations to standard procedures.

claim: P-values for the fold change were calculated using a bootstrap approach.
source: We then calculated p-values for the fold change calculated for the combined iDUX4 samples using a bootstrap approach.
evidence: This claim describes the statistical method used in the analysis.

claim: A web tool was developed for easy visualization of the RNA-seq and proteomics data.
source: Finally, in order to enable researchers and patients in the FSHD community to access the data generated in this study, we developed a web tool for easy visualization of these data (screenshot shown in Figure 5). This tool can be freely accessed at https://dynamicrna.shinyapps.io/dataviz/.
evidence: This claim is supported by the description and screenshot shown in Figure 5.

claim: The web tool can be freely accessed at https://dynamicrna.shinyapps.io/dataviz/.
source: This tool can be freely accessed at https://dynamicrna.shinyapps.io/dataviz/.
evidence: This is a factual statement about data availability.

claim: Comparable gene expression profiles are produced when DUX4 is expressed either via a lentiviral vector or when an inducible transgene is integrated into the genome of a myoblast cell line.
source: We previously showed that comparable gene expression profiles, which accurately capture the transcriptome of FSHD cells, are produced when DUX4 is expressed either via a lentiviral vector or when an inducible transgene is integrated into the genome of a myoblast cell line (Jagannathan et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Jagannathan et al., 2016).

claim: Both DUX4 expression systems accurately capture the transcriptome of FSHD cells.
source: We previously showed that comparable gene expression profiles, which accurately capture the transcriptome of FSHD cells, are produced when DUX4 is expressed either via a lentiviral vector or when an inducible transgene is integrated into the genome of a myoblast cell line (Jagannathan et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Jagannathan et al., 2016).

claim: Both DUX4 expression systems were used to corroborate results internally and ensure proteomic data were robust with respect to choice of model system.
source: Here, we used both of these expression systems to corroborate our results internally, thereby ensuring that our proteomic data were robust with respect to choice of model system.
evidence: This describes the experimental design rationale.

claim: MB135 myoblasts were cultured in SILAC labeling media for a week to establish labeling efficiency.
source: To this end, we cultured immortalized MB135 myoblasts in SILAC labeling media for a week and subjected the total protein from labeled cells, as well as a 1:1 mix of labeled to unlabeled cells, to mass spectrometry.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: The labeling time was increased to three weeks to achieve maximal SILAC labeling of MB135 myoblasts.
source: On the basis of these data, we proceeded with the labeling conditions and increased the labeling time even further (to three weeks) in order to achieve maximal SILAC labeling of the MB135 myoblasts.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure based on the labeling efficiency results.

claim: Samples were collected 24 hr and 36 hr post-transduction in the vDUX4 experiment.
source: MB135 myoblasts that had been adapted to light or heavy SILAC media for 3 weeks were transduced with lentivirus carrying DUX4 (vDUX4) or GFP (vGFP) expression constructs. Samples were collected 24 hr and 36 hr post-transduction.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: DUX4 expression was induced with 1 µg/ml of doxycycline for 14 hr in the iDUX4 experiment.
source: In an independent experiment, MB135 cells carrying a doxycycline-inducible DUX4 transgene (iDUX4; Jagannathan et al., 2016) were adapted to SILAC media for 3 weeks before DUX4 expression was induced with 1 µg/ml of doxycycline for 14 hr in two replicates carrying heavy and light SILAC labels.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: The vDUX4 dataset has lower depth than the iDUX4 dataset.
source: Note the lower number of peptides (and hence quantified proteins) from the vDUX4 sample, which indicates the lower depth of this dataset and yet yields fold changes that are highly consistent with those from the higher-depth iDUX4 dataset.
evidence: This is based on the number of peptides quantified in each dataset.

claim: The vDUX4 dataset yields fold changes that are highly consistent with those from the iDUX4 dataset.
source: Note the lower number of peptides (and hence quantified proteins) from the vDUX4 sample, which indicates the lower depth of this dataset and yet yields fold changes that are highly consistent with those from the higher-depth iDUX4 dataset.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of fold changes between the two datasets.
